{{Short description|Area of mathematics}}
{{more footnotes needed|date=April 2014}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''representation theory of the symmetric group''' is a particular case of the [[representation theory of finite groups]], for which a concrete and detailed theory can be obtained. This has a large area of potential applications, from [[symmetric function]] theory to [[quantum chemistry]] studies of atoms, molecules and solids.<ref>Philip R. Bunker and Per Jensen (1998) 
''Molecular Symmetry and Spectroscopy'', 2nd ed.  NRC Research Press, Ottawa 
[https://volumesdirect.com/products/molecular-symmetry-and-spectroscopy?_pos=1&_sid=ed0cc0319&_ss=r]
pp.198-202.{{ISBN|9780660196282}}</ref><ref>R.Pauncz (1995) ''The Symmetric Group in Quantum Chemistry'',
CRC Press, Boca Raton, Florida</ref>

The [[symmetric group]] S<sub>''n''</sub> has [[order of a group|order]] ''n''!. Its [[conjugacy class]]es are labeled by [[integer partition|partition]]s of ''n''. Therefore according to the representation theory of a finite group, the number of inequivalent [[irreducible representation]]s, over the [[complex number]]s, is equal to the number of partitions of ''n''. Unlike the general situation for finite groups, there is in fact a natural way to parametrize irreducible representations by the same set that parametrizes conjugacy classes, namely by partitions of ''n'' or equivalently [[Young diagram]]s of size ''n''.

Each such irreducible representation can in fact be realized over the [[integer]]s (every permutation acting by a matrix with integer entries); it can be explicitly constructed by computing the [[Young symmetrizer]]s acting on a space generated by the [[Young tableau]]x of shape given by the Young diagram. The dimension <math>d_\lambda</math> of the representation that corresponds to the Young diagram <math>\lambda</math> is given by the [[hook length formula]].

To each irreducible representation ρ we can associate an irreducible character, χ<sup>ρ</sup>.
To compute χ<sup>ρ</sup>(π) where π is a permutation, one can use the combinatorial [[Murnaghan–Nakayama rule]]
.<ref>Richard Stanley, ''Enumerative Combinatorics, Vol. 2''</ref> Note that χ<sup>ρ</sup> is constant on conjugacy classes,
that is, χ<sup>ρ</sup>(π) = χ<sup>ρ</sup>(σ<sup>−1</sup>πσ) for all permutations σ.

Over other [[field (mathematics)|field]]s, the situation can become much more complicated.  If the field ''K'' has [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] equal to zero or greater than ''n'' then by [[Maschke's theorem]] the [[group ring|group algebra]] ''K''S<sub>''n''</sub> is [[semisimple ring|semisimple]]. In these cases the irreducible representations defined over the integers give the complete set of irreducible representations (after reduction modulo the characteristic if necessary).

However, the irreducible representations of the symmetric group are not known in arbitrary characteristic. In this context it is more usual to use the language of [[module (mathematics)|module]]s rather than representations. The representation obtained from an irreducible representation defined over the integers by reducing modulo the characteristic will not in general be irreducible. The modules so constructed are called ''[[Specht modules]]'', and every irreducible does arise inside some such module. There are now fewer irreducibles, and although they can be classified they are very poorly understood. For example, even their [[dimension (vector space)|dimension]]s are not known in general.

The determination of the irreducible modules for the symmetric group over an arbitrary field is widely regarded as one of the most important [[open problem]]s in representation theory.

== Low-dimensional representations ==
=== Symmetric groups ===
The lowest-dimensional representations of the symmetric groups can be described explicitly,<ref>{{Citation | last1=Burnside | first1=William | author1-link=William Burnside 
| title=Theory of groups of finite order | publisher=[[Dover Publications]] 
| location=New York |mr=0069818 | year=1955}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Rasala | first1=Richard | title=On the minimal degrees of characters of Sn | doi=10.1016/0021-8693(77)90366-0 |mr=0427445 | year=1977| journal=Journal of Algebra | issn=0021-8693 | volume=45 | issue=1 | pages=132–181
| doi-access=free }}</ref> and over arbitrary fields.{{sfn|James|Kerber|1981}}{{page needed|date=April 2022}} The smallest two degrees in characteristic zero are described here:

Every symmetric group has a one-dimensional representation called the '''trivial representation''', where every element acts as the one by one [[identity matrix]].  For {{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 2}}, there is another irreducible representation of degree 1, called the '''sign representation''' or '''alternating character''', which takes a permutation to the one by one matrix with entry ±1 based on the [[sign of a permutation|sign of the permutation]].  These are the only one-dimensional representations of the symmetric groups, as one-dimensional representations are abelian, and the [[abelianization]] of the symmetric group is C<sub>2</sub>, the [[cyclic group]] of order 2.

For all ''n'', there is an ''n''-dimensional representation of the symmetric group of order ''n''!, called the '''{{visible anchor|natural permutation representation}}''', which consists of permuting ''n'' coordinates.  This has the trivial subrepresentation consisting of vectors whose coordinates are all equal.  The [[orthogonal complement]] consists of those vectors whose coordinates sum to zero, and when {{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 2}}, the representation on this subspace is an {{nowrap|(''n'' − 1)}}-dimensional irreducible representation, called the '''standard representation'''.  Another {{nowrap|(''n'' − 1)}}-dimensional irreducible representation is found by tensoring with the sign representation. An [[exterior power]] <math>\Lambda^k V</math> of the standard representation <math>V</math> is irreducible provided <math>0\leq k\leq n-1</math> {{harv|Fulton|Harris|2004}}.

For {{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 7}}, these are the lowest-dimensional irreducible representations of S<sub>''n''</sub> – all other irreducible representations have dimension at least ''n''.  However for {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 4}}, the surjection from S<sub>4</sub> to S<sub>3</sub> allows S<sub>4</sub> to inherit a two-dimensional irreducible representation.  For {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 6}}, the exceptional transitive embedding of S<sub>5</sub> into S<sub>6</sub> produces another pair of five-dimensional irreducible representations.

=== Alternating groups ===
[[File:Compound of five tetrahedra.png|thumb|The [[compound of five tetrahedra]], on which A<sub>5</sub> acts, giving a 3-dimensional representation.]]
The representation theory of the [[alternating group]]s is similar, though the sign representation disappears. For {{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 7}}, the lowest-dimensional irreducible representations are the [[trivial representation]] in dimension one, and the {{nowrap|(''n'' − 1)}}-dimensional representation from the other summand of the permutation representation, with all other irreducible representations having higher dimension, but there are exceptions for smaller ''n''.

The alternating groups for {{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 5}} have only one one-dimensional irreducible representation, the trivial representation.  For {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 3, 4}} there are two additional one-dimensional irreducible representations, corresponding to maps to the cyclic group of order&nbsp;3: {{nowrap|A<sub>3</sub> ≅ C<sub>3</sub>}} and {{nowrap|A<sub>4</sub> → A<sub>4</sub>/''V'' ≅ C<sub>3</sub>}}.

* For {{nowrap|''n'' ≥ 7}}, there is just one irreducible representation of degree {{nowrap|''n'' − 1}}, and this is the smallest degree of a non-trivial irreducible representation.
* For {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 3}} the obvious analogue of the {{nowrap|(''n'' − 1)}}-dimensional representation is reducible – the permutation representation coincides with the [[regular representation]], and thus breaks up into the three one-dimensional representations, as {{nowrap|A<sub>3</sub> ≅ C<sub>3</sub>}} is abelian; see the [[discrete Fourier transform]] for representation theory of cyclic groups.
* For {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 4}}, there is just one {{nowrap|''n'' − 1}} irreducible representation, but there are the exceptional irreducible representations of dimension&nbsp;1.
* For {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 5}}, there are two dual irreducible representations of dimension 3, corresponding to its action as [[icosahedral symmetry]].
* For {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 6}}, there is an extra irreducible representation of dimension 5 corresponding to the exceptional transitive embedding of ''A''<sub>5</sub> in&nbsp;''A''<sub>6</sub>.

==Tensor products of representations==

===Kronecker coefficients===

The [[tensor product of representations|tensor product]] of two representations of <math>S_n</math> corresponding to the Young diagrams <math>\lambda,\mu</math> is a combination of irreducible representations of <math>S_n</math>,
:<math>
V_\lambda\otimes V_\mu \cong \sum_\nu C_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} V_\nu
</math>
The coefficients <math>C_{\lambda\mu\nu}\in\mathbb{N}</math> are called the '''Kronecker coefficients''' of the symmetric group.
They can be computed from the [[character theory|characters]] of the representations {{harv|Fulton|Harris|2004}}:
:<math>
C_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} = \sum_\rho \frac{1}{z_\rho} \chi_\lambda(C_\rho)\chi_\mu(C_\rho)\chi_\nu(C_\rho)
</math>
The sum is over partitions <math>\rho</math> of <math>n</math>, with <math>C_\rho</math> the corresponding conjugacy classes. The values of the characters <math>\chi_\lambda(C_\rho)</math> can be computed using the [[Frobenius formula]]. The coefficients <math>z_\rho</math> are
:<math>
z_\rho = \prod_{j=0}^n j^{i_j}i_j! = \frac{n!}{|C_\rho|}
</math>
where <math>i_j</math> is the number of times <math>j</math> appears in <math>\rho</math>, so that <math>\sum i_jj = n</math>.

A few examples, written in terms of Young diagrams {{harv|Hamermesh|1989}}:
:<math>
(n - 1, 1) \otimes (n - 1, 1) \cong (n) + (n - 1, 1) + (n - 2, 2)
+ (n - 2, 1,1)
</math>
:<math>
(n - 1, 1) \otimes (n - 2, 2) \underset{n>4}{\cong} (n - 1, 1) + (n - 2, 2)
+ (n - 2, 1, 1) + (n - 3, 3)
+ (n - 3, 2, 1) 
</math>
:<math>
(n - 1, 1) \otimes (n - 2, 1,1) \cong (n - 1, 1) + (n - 2, 2) + (n - 2, 1,1)
+ (n - 3, 2, 1) + (n - 3, 1,1,1)
</math>
:<math>
\begin{align}
(n - 2, 2) \otimes (n - 2, 2) \cong & (n) + (n - 1, 1) + 2(n - 2, 2)
+ (n - 2, 1,1) + (n - 3, 3)
\\ & 
+ 2(n - 3, 2, 1) + (n - 3, 1,1,1)
+ (n - 4, 4) + (n - 4, 3, 1)
+ (n - 4, 2, 2)
\end{align}
</math>
There is a simple rule for computing <math>(n-1,1)\otimes \lambda</math> for any Young diagram <math>\lambda</math> {{harv|Hamermesh|1989}}: the result is the sum of all Young diagrams that are obtained from <math>\lambda</math> by removing one box and then adding one box, where the coefficients are one except for <math>\lambda</math> itself, whose coefficient is <math>\#\{\lambda_i\}-1</math>, i.e., the number of different row lengths minus one.

A constraint on the irreducible constituents of <math>V_\lambda\otimes V_\mu</math> is {{harv|James|Kerber|1981}}
:<math>
C_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}>0 \implies  |d_\lambda-d_\mu| \leq d_\nu \leq d_\lambda+d_\mu
</math>
where the depth <math>d_\lambda=n-\lambda_1</math> of a Young diagram is the number of boxes that do not belong to the first row.

===Reduced Kronecker coefficients===
For <math>\lambda</math> a Young diagram and <math>n\geq \lambda_1</math>, <math>\lambda[n]=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda)</math> is a Young diagram of size <math>n</math>. Then <math>C_{\lambda[n],\mu[n],\nu[n]}</math> is a bounded, non-decreasing function of <math>n</math>, and 
:<math>
\bar{C}_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} = \lim_{n\to\infty} C_{\lambda[n],\mu[n],\nu[n]}
</math>
is called a '''reduced Kronecker coefficient'''<ref name="bor09"/> or '''stable Kronecker coefficient'''.<ref name="as18"/> There are known bounds on the value of <math>n</math> where <math>C_{\lambda[n],\mu[n],\nu[n]}</math> reaches its limit.<ref name="bor09"/> The reduced Kronecker coefficients are structure constants of Deligne categories of representations of <math>S_n</math> with <math>n\in \mathbb{C}-\mathbb{N}</math>.<ref name="ent14"/>

In contrast to Kronecker coefficients, reduced Kronecker coefficients are defined for any triple of Young diagrams, not necessarily of the same size. If <math>|\nu|=|\lambda|+|\mu|</math>, then <math>\bar{C}_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}</math> coincides with the [[Littlewood-Richardson coefficient]] <math>c_{\lambda,\mu}^\nu</math>.<ref name="Dvir91"/> Reduced Kronecker coefficients can be written as linear combinations of Littlewood-Richardson coefficients via a change of bases in the space of symmetric functions, giving rise to expressions that are manifestly integral although not manifestly positive.<ref name="as18"/> Reduced Kronecker coefficients can also be written in terms of Kronecker and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients <math>c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta\gamma}</math>  via Littlewood's formula<ref name="lit58"/><ref name="oz17"/>
:<math>
\bar{C}_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} = \sum_{\lambda',\mu',\nu',\alpha,\beta,\gamma} C_{\lambda',\mu',\nu'} c^{\lambda}_{\lambda'\beta\gamma} c^{\mu}_{\mu'\alpha\gamma} c^\nu_{\nu'\alpha\beta}
</math>
Conversely, it is possible to recover the Kronecker coefficients as linear combinations of reduced Kronecker coefficients.<ref name="bor09"/>

Reduced Kronecker coefficients are implemented in the [[computer algebra system]] [[SageMath]].<ref name="oz15"/><ref name="sage"/>

==Eigenvalues of complex representations==

Given an element <math>w\in S_n</math> of cycle-type <math>\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots,\mu_k)</math> and order <math>m=\text{lcm}(\mu_i)</math>, the eigenvalues of <math>w</math> in a [[complex representation]] of <math>S_n</math> are of the type <math>\omega^{e_j}</math> with <math>\omega=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{m}}</math>, where the integers <math>e_j\in \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{m\mathbb{Z}}</math> are called the '''cyclic exponents''' of <math>w</math> with respect to the representation.<ref name="ste89"/>

There is a combinatorial description of the cyclic exponents of the symmetric group (and [[wreath product]]s thereof). Defining <math>\left(b_\mu(1),\dots,b_\mu(n)\right) = \left(\frac{m}{\mu_1},2\frac{m}{\mu_1},\dots, m, \frac{m}{\mu_2},2\frac{m}{\mu_2},\dots, m,\dots\right)</math>, let the <math>\mu</math>-index of a [[Young tableau#Tableaux|standard Young tableau]] be the sum of the values of <math>b_\mu</math> over the tableau's descents, <math>\text{ind}_\mu(T) = \sum_{k\in \{\text{descents}(T)\}} b_\mu(k)\bmod m</math>.
Then the cyclic exponents of the representation of <math>S_n</math> described by the Young diagram <math>\lambda</math> are the <math>\mu</math>-indices of the corresponding Young tableaux.<ref name="ste89"/>

In particular, if <math> w </math> is of order <math>n</math>, then <math>b_\mu(k)=k</math>, and <math>\text{ind}_\mu(T)</math> coincides with the major index of <math>T</math> (the sum of the descents). The cyclic exponents of an irreducible representation of <math>S_n</math> then describe [[Restricted representation|how it decomposes]] into representations of the [[cyclic group]] <math> \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{n\mathbb{Z}}</math>, with <math>\omega^{e_j}</math> being interpreted as the image of <math>w</math> in the (one-dimensional) representation characterized by <math>e_j</math>.
